rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every insect in this group that has been measured sees far less fine detail than that. If you are a large white butterfly, you read about a quarter of a cycle a degree, if you are a drone fly about half a cycle, and if you are a common green darner dragonfly about 2. For most other species, including the monarch, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Left out interommatidial angles because the acuity figures already make the comparison.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and the eyes of the butterfly Danaus chrysippus, a relative of the monarch, still follow it at 165 to 210 flashes a second. Nobody has measured how fast your eyes follow a flicker unless you are in that genus or one of the few other species tested, and that figure stays with the species it was measured in.
rows.note: Left out other species' flicker figures because they cannot travel to this view's other species; no record gives a speed for most of the 1,200 species.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Monarchs, cabbage whites, small tortoiseshells and LD moths each have a color-sensing cell that senses ultraviolet best, and so do the drone fly, the seven-spotted ladybird, a dragonfly, a damselfly and the brown marmorated stink bug. You very likely have one as well. Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all.
rows.note: No wavelength numbers used, since they have no comparison job here and do not carry between species.
